title: 道德經 第七十五章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 75, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 90. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 75 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 貪損 (What Greed Costs). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
民之饑，
以其上食稅之多，
是以饑。
民之難治，
以其上之有為，
是以難治。
民之輕死，
以其上求生之厚，
是以輕死。
夫唯無以生為者，
是賢於貴生。

morph.gloss: the people, the common folk — the ruled, as against those who rule them
(particle) coming between a subject and what is said of it, and turning the whole clause into a topic: 'the people's starving'
to starve; famine — properly a failed harvest, not an appetite
those above — the men over them; the ruler and his officers
to eat, to eat up (read shí; read sì the same character is 'to feed another')
the tax, the grain levy taken off the harvest
's — genitive again, now inside the clause: the muchness OF their eating of taxes
much, a great deal — the adjective standing as a noun, 'the muchness'
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither 是 'this' nor 以 'by means of' gives you it alone
hard to, difficult to (nán) — standing before a verb it says the verb is hard to do
to govern, to bring into order
's — the plain genitive, joining possessor to what is possessed: their superiors' having-action
to have, to be given to
doing, deliberate action (wéi) — the exact opposite of the book's 無為, acting without forcing
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither 是 'this' nor 以 'by means of' gives you it alone
to make light of, to treat as weighing nothing — the adjective 'light' working as a verb
to seek, to go looking for
's — the thickness OF their seeking of life
thick, laid on richly — what has too much body to it (adjective as noun)
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither 是 'this' nor 以 'by means of' gives you it alone
now, as for — the particle that opens a general observation (fú, not the noun fū 'a man')
to have no, to be without
to make anything of it, to do (wéi) — see the note: 無以…為 is a set frame
the one who — turns what precedes into a noun
this one (the demonstrative — NOT a verb 'to be'; Chinese has none)
worthier, of more worth (the adjective, with 於 supplying the 'than')
than (the all-purpose preposition, standing after the adjective)
to prize, to treat as precious

sentences.l:
The people's starving:
because of the muchness of their superiors' eating of taxes —
therefore they starve.
The people's being hard to govern:
because of their superiors' having-action —
therefore they are hard to govern.
The people's making light of death:
because of the thickness of their superiors' seeking of life —
therefore they make light of death.
Now it is only the one who makes nothing of living —
this one is worthier than prizing life.
sentences.i: The people starve because those above them eat up too much in taxes — that is why they starve. The people are hard to govern because those above them are forever doing something — that is why they are hard to govern. The people make light of dying because those above them pursue their own living too richly — that is why they make light of dying. It is precisely the one who makes nothing of his own living who is worth more than the one who prizes it.
sentences.n:
Three parallel triads, all built on one piece of grammar. 民之饑 is not 'the people's famine' in the sense of a thing they own: put 之 between a subject and what is said of it and the whole clause turns into a noun — 'the-people-starving'. That is what this chapter states, three times, and then explains. You will meet the construction constantly; chapter 78 uses it again in 弱之勝強, 'the-weak-overcoming-the-strong'.

上, 'those above', is who the chapter blames, and it never says 'king'. Wang Bi is blunter than the text: the people's going crooked and the government's falling into disorder, he says, all come from above and not from below — 皆由上，不由其下 — because the people follow those above them.

食稅 is literal. 稅 is the grain levy taken off the harvest, and the ruler eats it: the same food, off the same fields, in a different mouth. The three charges climb — his eating, his meddling, his own comfortable life — and the third is the one the chapter turns on.

有為, 'having-doing', is the exact negative of the book's 無為, acting without forcing. A ruler with 有為 is not wicked; he is busy.

輕死 answers the chapter before this one, which opens 民不畏死, 'the people do not fear death'. Here is the reason: when those above are living that richly off you, dying costs you less than it should.

The last couplet is the hard one, and honest readers differ. 無以生為 uses a set frame of the old language — 何以…為, 'what use is X?' — in which 以 carries the thing and 為 is the doing: to make nothing of X, to have no use for it. So: the one who does not make a business of living. Read 為 instead as wèi, 'for the sake of', and you get 'the one who does not act for the sake of his life', which arrives at the same place by another road; we read wéi, following the house default. Then 是 is the demonstrative 'this one' — not a copula — and 於 after 賢 supplies the 'than' that the bare adjective cannot, the same frame as chapter 69's 禍莫大於.

The Mawangdui silk manuscripts set a final 也 after each topic clause here, and the first cause is reported there as 取食稅, 'the taking of the grain-tax', spelling out what the received text leaves implied.
